provenance: Synthetic numerical examples; official OpenStax University Physics Volume 1 section links. This file contains independently specified target answers; NO measured data or runtime changes.

cases.question: A rover moves from x=10 m to x=34 m in 6 s; what is its signed mean velocity?
cases.lab: Plot x at the two endpoints and insert an intermediate detour; recompute mean velocity
cases.misconception: Treating the 24 m endpoint displacement as total path length without checking reversals
cases.boundary: The 4 m/s mean does not imply constant instantaneous speed.

cases.question: A 3 kg puck moves west at 5 m/s (east positive); what signed linear momentum does it carry?
cases.lab: Reverse the puck's measured direction while retaining mass and compare signed impulses
cases.misconception: Dropping the negative direction when multiplying positive mass by velocity
cases.boundary: Mass is constant and speed is nonrelativistic; a vector axis must be specified.

cases.question: Two horizontal pulls of +9 N and -9 N act on a cart; what resultant force disproves the claim that motion must stop?
cases.lab: Sketch two force arrows and test both an initially moving and an initially stationary cart
cases.misconception: A zero net force guarantees a zero velocity rather than zero acceleration
cases.boundary: Only a constant-mass inertial-frame model is claimed; actual drag may be nonzero.

cases.question: A frictionless glider initially travels at +2.5 m/s under zero net force for 8 s; what displacement follows?
cases.lab: Record equal-time position marks and compare their increments with a zero-force prediction
cases.misconception: A continuing force is required to sustain uniform translation
cases.boundary: Initial speed is assumed known; zero acceleration is a model assumption.

cases.question: A 12 kg test cart experiences a measured +36 N net push; what acceleration follows?
cases.lab: Balance an independent force table and reconstruct the 36 N from mass times acceleration
cases.misconception: Using an applied-force label when the 36 N is explicitly NET force
cases.boundary: Classical Newtonian translation, constant mass and inertial axes.

cases.question: A 9 kg cart has +50 N drive and 14 N opposing resistance; what is its acceleration?
cases.lab: Draw both arrows; compute net force independently as 36 N before dividing by mass
cases.misconception: Subtracting the resisting force with the wrong sign or dividing drive alone by mass
cases.boundary: Resistance is constant only over the modeled interval.

cases.question: A foot exerts +28 N on a force plate; what force does the plate exert on that foot?
cases.lab: Use paired contact-force readings and reverse the positive axis to test sign convention
cases.misconception: Putting equal-and-opposite contact forces on the same free-body diagram
cases.boundary: Third-law pair forces act on different bodies in the same interaction.

cases.question: Two carts of 6 kg and 12 kg interact at 48 N; what acceleration of the heavier cart is opposite to the force on the lighter cart?
cases.lab: Compute lighter-cart acceleration +8 m/s² separately; compare force reconstructions
cases.misconception: Claiming equal third-law forces imply equal accelerations despite unequal masses
cases.boundary: Each cart has no other horizontal force during the chosen interval.

cases.question: An ideal inverse-square gravitational attraction is 80 N at r; what is its magnitude at 2r?
cases.lab: Calculate F at r, 2r and 4r and graph F against 1/r²
cases.misconception: Doubling separation halves gravitational force, instead of quartering it
cases.boundary: Two point masses are fixed; ignore other bodies and finite-size effects.

cases.question: At a steady speed, a sled has +15 N propulsion and -15 N drag; what net force is compatible with Newton's first law?
cases.lab: Compare matched 15 N force arrows; introduce +1 N unbalanced thrust and predict response
cases.misconception: Treating the nonzero engine thrust as a nonzero net force
cases.boundary: Speed remains steady only if total forces, including unlisted forces, sum to zero.

cases.question: A moving 9 kg trolley feels 46 N traction and 10 N resistance; what acceleration tests a defective force sensor?
cases.lab: Predict acceleration using independent force/mass data; compute the force residual against 4 m/s²
cases.misconception: Accepting a 46/9 m/s² readout despite separately measured resistance
cases.boundary: The modeled resistance is treated as constant; report measurement tolerance separately.

cases.question: A force of +120 N acts for 0.15 s; what signed impulse is delivered to a pad?
cases.lab: Integrate a rectangular force-versus-time plot and compare the area with 18 N·s
cases.misconception: Confusing newtons with newton-seconds or interpreting impulse as final momentum without initial state
cases.boundary: Assumes force is constant in time; force sampling can reveal pulse shape.

cases.question: A projectile leaves level ground with v_x=14 m/s, v_y=9.8 m/s; what ideal level-ground range follows?
cases.lab: Predict flight time 2.0 s independently from vertical motion before computing horizontal range
cases.misconception: Using total launch speed as horizontal speed or omitting the return-to-height condition
cases.boundary: No aerodynamic drag, constant g=9.8 m/s², same launch and landing elevation.

cases.question: A 50 N push at a 0.40 m lever arm makes sin(theta)=0.5; what signed torque magnitude results?
cases.lab: Reconfigure the force to perpendicular and confirm the torque doubles to 20 N·m
cases.misconception: Using rF without the perpendicular-force factor sin(theta)
cases.boundary: Rigid lever and fixed pivot; sign needs an explicitly chosen rotation axis.

cases.question: A train slows from +14 to +2 m/s in 4 s; what signed mean acceleration describes braking?
cases.lab: Plot v endpoints and compare slope with the time-integrated acceleration
cases.misconception: Replacing signed acceleration -3 m/s² with +3 because speed changed by 12
cases.boundary: Average acceleration is not a peak braking acceleration.

cases.question: For synthetic v(t)=v0+6t-0.8t² (SI), what acceleration exists at t=5 s?
cases.lab: Compare central-difference slopes over ±0.1 s around t=5 against analytic -2 m/s²
cases.misconception: Substituting velocity itself for its time derivative
cases.boundary: Polynomial fits are not evidence of real-world acceleration outside calibrated domain.

cases.question: A rotor has I=0.75 kg·m² and angular rate +8 rad/s; what axial angular momentum follows?
cases.lab: Reconstruct I from independently specified L and ω and check SI units
cases.misconception: Confusing L=Iω with kinetic energy ½Iω²
cases.boundary: Rigid rotation about a principal fixed axis; inertia is treated constant.

cases.question: A motion logger records x=4 m at t=0 and x=26 m at t=11 s; what average signed velocity is observed?
cases.lab: Construct a nonuniform two-interval motion path with the same endpoints and duration
cases.misconception: Claiming 2 m/s must also be the velocity at every intermediate time
cases.boundary: The time origin is irrelevant to the interval average; precision limited by logger.

cases.question: A hiker walks +8 m then -3 m in a total of 5 s; what mean signed velocity follows?
cases.lab: Compute the 11 m average speed separately and contrast with +1 m/s velocity
cases.misconception: Dividing total traveled distance 11 m by time to claim signed velocity +2.2 m/s
cases.boundary: Segment durations are unspecified; only total mean velocity can be inferred.

cases.question: A sensor travels at constant 12 m/s around a circular path of radius 18 m; what inward acceleration has nonzero magnitude?
cases.lab: Draw velocity tangents at quadrature positions; compare change in direction with inward acceleration
cases.misconception: Claiming no acceleration because the speed magnitude is unchanged
cases.boundary: Uniform circular motion is assumed; angular speed is v/r.

cases.question: A lift platform begins at +3 m/s and accelerates at +2 m/s² for 5 s; what final velocity follows?
cases.lab: Compare a velocity-time graph intercept and slope; read the endpoint at 5 s
cases.misconception: Replacing v_f=v_i+at by v_f=at and dropping initial motion
cases.boundary: Acceleration is constant only within the modeled time interval.

cases.question: A constant 14 N force acts parallel to a 3 m displacement; how much mechanical work is done?
cases.lab: Calculate area under a constant force-versus-displacement graph, then change the angle to 90°
cases.misconception: Calculating 14/3 N/m and calling it joules
cases.boundary: Only the component of force parallel to displacement performs this work.

cases.question: A lab cart moves from x=+19 m to x=-7 m; what displacement encodes direction of travel?
cases.lab: Mark the origin and signed endpoints on a number line; inspect path independence
cases.misconception: Taking |x_f|+|x_i| as a positive signed displacement
cases.boundary: Total distance traveled cannot be reconstructed from endpoints alone.

cases.question: Three successive one-dimensional moves are +5 m, -12 m, and +4 m; what net displacement results?
cases.lab: Compare a three-arrow vector chain with an endpoint difference calculation
cases.misconception: Summing absolute segment distances 21 m as displacement
cases.boundary: Straight-line segments share a common coordinate axis; path length differs.

cases.question: Velocity changes from -3 m/s to +9 m/s over 6 s; what positive mean acceleration permits a turnaround?
cases.lab: Use the constant-acceleration special case to find the zero-velocity time 1.5 s
cases.misconception: Concluding positive acceleration means the object moved only east
cases.boundary: Endpoint velocities constrain an average, not the full velocity history.

cases.question: A moving body goes from +16 to -4 m/s in 5 s; what mean acceleration crosses zero velocity?
cases.lab: Graph the zero crossing at t=4 s for a constant -4 m/s² example
cases.misconception: Using speed change 12 m/s in place of vector velocity change -20 m/s
cases.boundary: A nonlinear real braking profile could share these endpoints.

cases.question: A 2 kg particle has tangential velocity 6 m/s at 0.5 m from the origin; what angular momentum magnitude follows?
cases.lab: Rotate the velocity vector toward the radius and confirm angular momentum trends to zero
cases.misconception: Using mvr when velocity is radial rather than perpendicular
cases.boundary: Velocity is perpendicular to radius for the numerical case; reference origin matters.

cases.question: A robot translates from x=12 m to x=3 m in 3 s; what signed average velocity should navigation report?
cases.lab: Check signed displacement -9 m and graph two distinct trajectories with same endpoints
cases.misconception: Reporting +3 m/s because speed cannot be negative
cases.boundary: Coordinates use right-positive axis; odometry bias is unmodeled.

cases.question: A buggy moves +7 m then -1 m in 2 s; what is its displacement-based average velocity?
cases.lab: Compute +6 m net displacement and compare to 8 m traveled
cases.misconception: Treating +7 and -1 as scalar distances and obtaining 4 m/s average speed
cases.boundary: No inference about peak speed follows from segment totals.

cases.question: A rotating arm tip travels at 9 m/s at radius 3 m; what centripetal acceleration is required?
cases.lab: Calculate ω=3 rad/s independently, then a_c=ω²r
cases.misconception: Using v/r=3 s⁻¹ as centripetal acceleration instead of angular rate
cases.boundary: Rigid circular path and steady angular speed; acceleration points radially inward.

cases.question: A particle starts with v0=+5 m/s and a=-2 m/s²; how much signed displacement accumulates in 3 s?
cases.lab: Integrate the linear velocity graph (trapezoid area) and obtain +6 m
cases.misconception: Using v0t+at² instead of the ½at² correction
cases.boundary: Acceleration is constant; direction reverses after t=2.5 s.

cases.question: A 4 kg cart travels at 3 m/s; what kinetic energy in joules checks a units mistake?
cases.lab: Compute ½·4·9 and compare with momentum 12 kg·m/s
cases.misconception: Using mv (12 kg·m/s) as though it were kinetic energy in J
cases.boundary: Classical kinetic energy; speed relative to specified reference frame.

cases.question: A route has orthogonal displacements +3 m east and +4 m north; what straight-line resultant magnitude follows?
cases.lab: Draw a scaled right triangle and verify 5 m using Pythagoras
cases.misconception: Adding orthogonal magnitudes to report 7 m net displacement
cases.boundary: Planar Euclidean geometry; vector magnitude discards direction quadrant.

cases.question: A probe reads x=-8 m initially and x=-19 m finally; what signed change confirms further leftward motion?
cases.lab: Mark both negative coordinates and check Δx + x_i = x_f
cases.misconception: Subtracting magnitudes 19-8 and overlooking negative direction
cases.boundary: This is a coordinate displacement, not uncertainty in sensor calibration.

cases.question: For x(t)=x0+2t-0.5t², what instantaneous velocity occurs at t=3 s?
cases.lab: Approximate a central secant with h=0.1 and 0.01 s around t=3 s
cases.misconception: Treating positive x(t)-x0 as proof velocity at 3 s remains positive
cases.boundary: Differentiability and SI coefficients required; noisy samples change numerical derivative.

cases.question: A 5 kg block receives +27 N and -7 N horizontal forces; what acceleration should its free-body diagram predict?
cases.lab: Sum horizontal arrows +20 N before using ΣF_x=ma_x
cases.misconception: Including the +27 N force twice after summing the arrows
cases.boundary: Vertical forces assumed balanced; block remains in inertial lab frame.

cases.question: A block slides down an incline with sinθ=0.6, cosθ=0.8 and μk=0.25; what downhill acceleration follows?
cases.lab: Compute downslope g·0.6=5.88 and opposing frictional acceleration g·0.25·0.8=1.96
cases.misconception: Taking μmg rather than μmgcosθ on the incline
cases.boundary: Kinetic sliding assumed, no external applied force, constant g=9.8 m/s².

cases.question: A 6 kg box is pulled vertically upward by 9 N but stays on a horizontal floor; what normal reaction remains?
cases.lab: Check vertical equilibrium N+9−58.8=0 N independently
cases.misconception: Assuming N=mg even while another upward force acts
cases.boundary: Contact is maintained and vertical acceleration is zero.

cases.question: An 8 kg crate slides horizontally with μk=0.35; what friction magnitude resists the motion?
cases.lab: Reconstruct N=78.4 N and multiply by 0.35; compare with force sensor
cases.misconception: Treating static-friction upper bound as equal to kinetic force in motion
cases.boundary: Kinetic friction coefficient constant; surface is level and speed nonzero.

cases.question: A tracked vehicle follows x(t)=x0+7t−0.5t²; what instantaneous velocity is indicated at t=4 s?
cases.lab: Compute symmetric secants about 4 s, shrinking h while holding center fixed
cases.misconception: Using the finite interval displacement over 4 s as instantaneous velocity
cases.boundary: Smooth polynomial idealization; sensor time stamps need synchronization.

cases.question: For x(t)=x0−2t+0.75t², what velocity at t=4 s distinguishes acceleration from speed?
cases.lab: Solve the turning time t=4/3 s and compare with +4 m/s at t=4 s
cases.misconception: Assuming initial negative velocity means velocity stays negative
cases.boundary: Quadratic model is local; coefficients have SI units m/s and m/s².

cases.question: A vehicle at +18 m/s brakes with constant acceleration -3 m/s²; when does it first stop?
cases.lab: Predict the zero of v(t)=18−3t, then evaluate at t=5 and t=7 s
cases.misconception: Interpreting negative acceleration as an immediately negative velocity
cases.boundary: No reversal before stopping is assumed; braking magnitude is constant.

cases.question: A 2 kg cart at +6 m/s sticks to a 4 kg cart at -1 m/s; what shared final velocity satisfies momentum conservation?
cases.lab: Compute total initial momentum +8 kg·m/s then divide by total mass 6 kg
cases.misconception: Conserving kinetic energy during a perfectly inelastic collision
cases.boundary: Neglects external horizontal impulse; mechanical energy is not conserved.

cases.question: A puck glides left at 1.25 m/s with negligible net force for 12 s; what signed displacement results?
cases.lab: Mark uniformly spaced negative displacements at 3 s intervals
cases.misconception: Inferring zero motion because net force equals zero
cases.boundary: Uniform-velocity approximation ignores friction and air drag.

cases.question: A test stage has +11 N drive and -11 N friction; what net force does the first-law prediction require?
cases.lab: Check vector arrows; perturb friction to 10 N and recompute residual
cases.misconception: Adding force magnitudes 22 N instead of signed components
cases.boundary: The 0 N result does not establish absence of individual forces.

cases.question: A 9 kg robot platform has +63 N measured horizontal net force; what acceleration follows?
cases.lab: Estimate +7 m/s velocity change over 1 s if net force remains constant
cases.misconception: Confusing 63 N of force with 63 kg·m/s impulse
cases.boundary: No unmodeled rolling resistance beyond measured net force.

cases.question: A 7 kg payload must accelerate at +2.5 m/s²; what required net force must the actuator deliver?
cases.lab: Compute +17.5 N as target net, then add a hypothetical +3 N resistance separately
cases.misconception: Calling the required net force the complete actuator specification without accounting for drag
cases.boundary: Ideal translational dynamics; actuator must also compensate any external resistance.

cases.question: A hand applies +150 N to a ball for 0.08 s; what is the ball's impulse and the hand's opposite impulse?
cases.lab: Integrate the 0.08 s force pulse for each body with opposite signs
cases.misconception: Assigning +12 N·s to BOTH bodies despite third-law opposition
cases.boundary: Requires same contact interval and force magnitude; other impulses ignored.
